befog.e: Proto-Indo-European *h₁ep-der. Proto-Indo-European *h₁épsder. Proto-Indo-European *h₁epider. Proto-Indo-European *h₁pi Proto-Germanic *bider. Proto-Germanic *bi- Proto-West Germanic *bi- Old English be- Middle English bi- English be- English fog English befog From be- + fog.

d.g: make a fool or dupe of

befool.e: From Middle English bifolen, equivalent to be- + fool.

d.g: To make foul; to soil; to contaminate, pollute.
d.x: Only the four walls of his home still stood, blackened and smoking with the sluggish, stinking smoke that befouled the sea-wind.

d.g: To defecate on, to soil with excrement.
d.x: For its an ill Bird will befoule her own Nest […]

d.g: To stain or mar (e.g., with infamy or disgrace).
d.x: “[…] you combine a vulgar atheism and an iconoclastic desire to befoul the sacred ideas of the average man or woman, collectively scorned as the bourgeoisie——”

d.g: To entangle or run against so as to impede motion.
To become a friend of (someone), to make friends with (someone).
d.x: Good Seruilius, vvill you befriend mee ſo farre, as to vſe mine ovvne vvords to him?

d.g: To act as a friend to (someone, especially a client) by providing companionship and support; to assist, to help.
d.x: The social worker very clearly befriends the families with whom she works, and the GP becomes a friend to many of his patients.

d.g: To benefit or favour (someone or something); also, to advocate or promote (someone or something).
d.x: Hence therefore, euery leader to his charge, / For on their anſvvere vvill vve ſet on them, / And God befriend vs as our cauſe is juſt.

d.g: To perplex, confuse (someone).
d.x: The explanation left him completely befuddled.

d.g: To stupefy (someone), especially with alcohol.
d.x: […] to the American and French alcoholics, who drink in order to get drunk and befuddle the brain

befuddle.e: Proto-Indo-European *h₁ep-der. Proto-Indo-European *h₁épsder. Proto-Indo-European *h₁epider. Proto-Indo-European *h₁pi Proto-Germanic *bider. Proto-Germanic *bi- Proto-West Germanic *bi- Old English be- Middle English bi- English be- English fuddle English befuddle From be- + fuddle.

d.g: To request the help of someone, often in the form of money.
d.x: He begged on the street corner from passers-by.

d.g: To plead with someone for help, a favor, etc.; to entreat.
d.x: I beg your pardon. I didn’t mean to cause offence.

d.g: To unwillingly provoke a negative, often violent, reaction.
d.x: The way you keep eating raw meat, you're just begging to get tapeworms.

d.g: To obviously lack or be in need of something.
d.x: A captivating novel that just begs for a movie adaptation

d.g: A pretentious, attention-seeking, or eccentric person.
d.x: Girls told me about not wanting to be seen by boys as "too much", "too loud", "weird", "annoying", a "pick me", or "a beg" (someone looking for attention). They told me how boys can be loud and funny, but that girls had better not.

beg.e: Inherited from Middle English beggen, of uncertain origin. Possibly from Old English *becgian, *bedcian, syncopated forms of bedecian (“to beg”), itself of obscure origin. …

d.g: To produce or bring forth (a child); to be a parent of; to father or sire.
d.x: The King intends to beget a child within the next five years.

d.g: To cause; to produce; to bring forth.
d.x: Wealth begets wealth; poverty begets poverty.

d.g: To happen to; befall.

beget.e: From Middle English begeten [influenced by Old Norse geta ("to get, to guess")], from Old English beġietan (“to get”), from Proto-Germanic *bigetaną (“to find, seize”), equivalent to be- + get. Cognate with Old Saxon bigetan (“to find, seize”), Old High German bigezan (“to gain, achieve, win, procure”).

d.g: To cover with gold, or to make golden (in color, or figuratively).
d.x: bride-laces begilt

d.g: To ingrain grime or dirt which is difficult to remove into (something); also (more generally), to make (something) dirty; to soil.
d.x: My name that vvas as freſh / As Dians Viſage, is novv begrim'd and blacke / As mine ovvne face.

begrime.e: From be- (prefix meaning ‘about; abundantly; all around; all over’) + grime (“to cake with dirt”).

d.g: To grudge about or over; be envious or covetous.
To be reluctant.
To give reluctantly.
d.x: Okay, then, next time you go and leave me stay here. See if I begrudge you a little fun.

begrudge.e: From Middle English bigrucchen (“to grumble at”), equivalent to be- (“at, about, over”) + grudge. Compare also English begrouch.

d.g: To deceive or delude (using guile).
d.x: I know, sir, I am no flatterer: he that beguiled you, in a plain accent, was a plain knave.

d.g: To charm, delight or captivate.
d.x: I will never touch The Orb, even though its mysterious glow seduces and beguiles.

d.g: To cause (time) to seem to pass quickly, by way of pleasant diversion.
d.x: We beguiled the hours away.

beguile.e: From Middle English begilen, begylen; equivalent to be- + guile. Compare Middle Dutch begilen (“to beguile”). Doublet of bewile.

d.g: To conduct (oneself) well, or in a given way; to conform.
d.x: You need to behave yourself, young lady.

d.g: To act, conduct oneself in a specific manner; used with an adverbial of manner.
d.x: He behaves like a child whenever she's around.

d.g: To act in a polite or proper way.
d.x: His mother threatened to spank him if he didn't behave.

behave.e: Proto-Indo-European *h₁ep-der. Proto-Indo-European *h₁épsder. Proto-Indo-European *h₁epider. Proto-Indo-European *h₁pi Proto-Germanic *bider. Proto-Germanic *bi- Proto-West Germanic *bi- Proto-Indo-European *kap-der. …

d.g: To deliberately remove the head of; to cut off (someone's) head.
d.x:
“For a while it was hand-to-hand between us,
then blood went curling along the currents
and I beheaded Grendel's mother in the hall
with a mighty sword.”]

behead.e: From Middle English beheden, bihefden, biheveden, from Old English behēafdian (“to behead”), equivalent to be- (“off, away”) + head.

d.g: To look at or see (someone or something), especially appreciatively; to descry, to look upon.
To contemplate (someone or something).
To look.
d.x: Lo and behold.

d.g: look, a call of attention to something

behold.e: From Middle English biholden, from Old English behealdan (“to hold, possess, preserve, belong, keep, observe, look at, take care, beware, be cautious, restrain, act, behave”), from Proto-West Germanic *bihaldan (“to hold with, keep”), equivalent to be- + hold. …

d.g: To befit, be appropriate or necessary to somebody. Alternative form of behove.
d.x: It ill behooves my mother to complain.

d.g: To be fitting.
d.x: Now, while discoursing of sperm, it behooves to speak of other things akin to it, in the business of preparing the sperm whale for the try-works.

d.g: To befit, to suit.
d.x: I never over Horeb heard / The blast of advent blow; / No fire-faced prophet brought me word / Which way behoved me go.

d.g: To be necessary for (someone).
To be in the best interest of; to benefit.
To be needful, meet or becoming.

behove.e: From Middle English behoven, bihoven (“to be necessary, requisite; to be compelled or required (to do something)”), from Old English behōfian (“to need; to be necessary”), from Proto-Germanic *bihōfōną (“to benefit, behove, need”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *kap- (“to grab, seize”). …

d.g: To decorate or bedeck with jewels or gems.
d.x: They bejewel each other beautifully to promote their evil cause.

bejewel.e: Proto-Indo-European *h₁ep-der. Proto-Indo-European *h₁épsder. Proto-Indo-European *h₁epider. Proto-Indo-European *h₁pi Proto-Germanic *bider. Proto-Germanic *bi- Proto-West Germanic *bi- Old English be- Middle English bi- English be- English jewel English bejewel From be- (“on, about, all over”) + jewel.

d.g: US spelling of belabour.

belabor.e: From be- (“on, upon, about, over”) + labor.

d.g: To beat or thump (someone) soundly.
d.x: [F]ew country people there are who do not love to see two sturdy fellows thwack and belabour each other with quarter-staff, single-stick, or fists.

d.g: To attack (someone) verbally.
To discuss or explain (something) excessively or repeatedly; to harp on or overelaborate.
d.x:
1961, John Fitzgerald Kennedy, inaugural speech
Let both sides explore what problems unite us instead of belabouring those problems which divide us.

belabour.e: From be- (“on, upon, about, over”) + labour. Compare bework, betoil, beswink.

d.g: To besiege; to surround with troops.
To vex, harass, or beset.
To exhaust.

beleaguer.e: Borrowed from Dutch belegeren and/or Middle Low German belēgeren; equivalent to be- + lair. Compare also German belagern, Danish belejre. The English spelling was perhaps influenced by unrelated league.

d.g: To give a false representation of.
d.x: Her smooth complexion and dark hair belie her actual age.

d.g: To contradict, to show (something) to be false.
d.x: Her obvious nervousness belied what she said.

d.g: To call a liar; to accuse of falsehood.
d.x: They haue belyed the Lord, and ſaid; It is not he, neither ſhall euill come vpon vs, neither ſhal we ſee ſwoꝛd noꝛ famine.

d.g: To fill with lies; to lie to.

belie.e: From Middle English belyen, beliggen, from Old English beliċġan, biliċġan (“to lie around, surround, hedge in, encompass”), from Proto-West Germanic *biliggjan, from Proto-Germanic *biligjaną (“to lie around”). Equivalent to be- (“around, by”) + lie (“to be positioned”).

d.g: To accept as true, particularly without absolute certainty (i.e., as opposed to knowing).
d.x: If you believe the numbers, you'll agree we need change.

d.g: To accept that someone is telling the truth.
d.x: Why did I ever believe you?

d.g: To have been convinced by rational means to accept the truth of a proposition.
To have been influenced by arational means (such as emotional experience, the imagination of need, etc.) to accept the truth of a proposition.

believe.e: Proto-Indo-European *h₁ep-der. Proto-Indo-European *h₁épsder. Proto-Indo-European *h₁epider. Proto-Indo-European *h₁pi Proto-Germanic *bider. Proto-Germanic *bi- Proto-West Germanic *bi- Proto-Indo-European *lewbʰ-der. …

d.g: To knowingly say that (someone or something) is smaller or less important than it actually is, especially as a way of showing contempt or deprecation.
d.x: Don't belittle your colleagues.

d.g: To make small.
d.x: Now, the big blue space of river and sky belittled him, ulled him back into bewildered childhood.

belittle.e: From be- + little. Coined by Thomas Jefferson in 1782.

d.g: A deep, hearty laugh
To have its proper place.
d.x: Where does this book belong? It belongs on the top shelf.

d.g: To be accepted in a group.
d.x: You don’t belong here — get out.

d.g: To be a part of a group.
d.x: I don’t belong to the Southside Crew.

d.g: To be the property of, or be bound to by dependency or as an attribute.
d.x: That house belongs to me.

d.g: To live in or be from a place.
d.x: " We have," he says, "in these parts a provincial usage of the word "belong:" as, "belong to Halifax," "belong to Leeds: "or, more commonly, "belong Halifax," "belong Leeds:" meaning, live there.

d.g: To stain or mar, as with infamy or disgrace; to tarnish; to sully.

bemire.e: From Middle English *bemyren (possibly attested in Middle English bemyred), equivalent to be- (“all over”) + mire.

d.g: To moan or complain about (something).
d.x: He bemoaned the drought but went on watering his lawn.

d.g: To be dismayed or worried about (someone), particularly because of their situation or what has happened to them.
d.x:
Son. Was ever son so rued a father’s death?
Father. Was ever father so bemoan’d his son?

bemoan.e: From Middle English bemenen, bimenen, from Old English bemǣnan (“to bemoan, bewail, lament”); equivalent to be- (“about, concerning”) + moan. Alteration of vowel from Middle to Modern English due to analogy with moan.

d.g: To mock repeatedly; flout.
To cause to appear as if mock or unreal; excel or surpass, as the genuine surpasses the counterfeit.
To confuse or bewilder.
d.x: [With] fairy tales bemused the shepherd lies.

d.g: To be amused, especially sardonically.
To devote to the Muses.
d.x: When those incorrigible things, Poets, are once irrecoverably Be-mus'd

d.g: To make drunk; to intoxicate.
d.x: a parson much be-mus'd in beer

bemuse.e: From be- + muse. In meaning, influenced by bemaze and later amuse.

d.g: reproduce by the Benday process
To benefit; to act as benefactor toward.
d.x: You must feel yourselves in the Christian economy on one great level , each benefacting the other , without assuming superiority one over the other.

d.g: To reduce (ores or other raw materials)

beneficiate.e: Spanish beneficiarbor. English beneficiate Borrowed from Spanish beneficiar (“to benefit, to work mines”).

d.g: subject to a reduction process
overtake with darkness or night

benight.e: From Middle English benyghten, binighten, bynyȝten, equivalent to be- + night.

d.g: To make numb, as by cold or anesthetic.
d.x: […] the sayd Phillip […] in the same his pilgrimage was stricken with such colde, that he fell into a palsey, and was benumbed of the right side of his body.

d.g: To deaden, dull (the mind, faculties, etc.).
d.x: I struggled, and trembled, and was so benumb’d with Terror, that I sunk down, not in a Fit, and yet not myself […]

benumb.e: Proto-Indo-European *h₁ep-der. Proto-Indo-European *h₁épsder. Proto-Indo-European *h₁epider. Proto-Indo-European *h₁pi Proto-Germanic *bider. Proto-Germanic *bi- Proto-West Germanic *bi- Old English be- Middle English bi- English be- English numb English benumb From be- + numb.

d.g: To plaster over; to cover or smear thickly; to bedaub (with something).
d.x: He pelted straight on in his socks, beplastered with filth out of all semblance to a human being.

beplaster.e: Proto-Indo-European *h₁ep-der. Proto-Indo-European *h₁épsder. Proto-Indo-European *h₁epider. Proto-Indo-European *h₁pi Proto-Germanic *bider. Proto-Germanic *bi- Proto-West Germanic *bi- Old English be- Middle English bi- English be- English plaster English beplaster From be- + plaster.

d.g: To give or leave by will; to give by testament.
To hand down; to transmit.
d.x: Ownership of manufacturing workshops is not essential to that job; but BR happen to have been bequeathed a considerable number with a proud history.

d.g: To give; to offer; to commit.

bequeath.e: From Middle English biquethen, from Old English becweþan (“to say, to speak, to address, exhort, admonish, blame, bequeath, leave by will”). Cognate with Old Frisian biquetha.

d.g: To chide or scold vehemently.
d.x: What society tells people that they can “do whatever they want” to dissidents, and yet berates anyone for treating them well?

berate.e: Proto-Indo-European *h₁ep-der. Proto-Indo-European *h₁épsder. Proto-Indo-European *h₁epider. Proto-Indo-European *h₁pi Proto-Germanic *bider. Proto-Germanic *bi- Proto-West Germanic *bi- Old English be- Middle English bi- English be- English rate English berate From be- + rate (“to scold, upbraid”).

d.g: To deprive by or as if by violence; to rob; to strip.
d.x: Madam, you have bereft me of all words,

d.g: To deprive of power; prevent.
To take away someone or something that is important or close; deprive.
d.x: Death bereaved him of his wife.

d.g: To destroy life; cut off.

bereave.e: Inherited from Middle English bireven, from Old English berēafian (“to bereave, deprive of, take away, seize, rob, despoil”), from Proto-Germanic *biraubōną, and Old English berēofan (“to bereave, deprive, rob of”); both equivalent to be- + reave. …

d.g: To beseech someone or something for something.
d.x: after what manner, I beseech you, must the mind proceed in this operation?

beseech.e: From Middle English besechen, bisechen, prefixed form of Old English sēċan (“to seek or inquire about”); compare the doublet beseek, from the same dialect that gave seek. …

d.g: accord or comport with

beseem.e: PIE word *h₁epi From Middle English bisemen (“to beseem”) [and other forms], from be-, bi- (prefix forming transitive verbs with a completive, figurative, or intensifying sense) + semen (“to seem; to be or see as appropriate; to be visible or apparent; to regard”). …

d.g: To assail or attack (someone) from all sides; to set about.
To occupy and block (an entrance, a passage, etc.), especially to prevent people from passing.
To decorate (someone or something) by surrounding with accessories, etc.
Of dangers, difficulties, enemies, etc.: to negatively affect (someone or something); to trouble.
d.x: Track and platforms have been upgraded, but refurbished trains from Vivarail have been beset by software problems.

beset.e: From Middle English besetten, bisetten (“to besiege, blockade; to fill, occupy; to harass, beset; to allot, bestow; to arrange, manage; to place, set; to provide for; to treat in a certain way”), from Old English besettan, bisettan (“to surround, beset; to set near; etc.”), from Proto-West Germanic *bisattjan, from Pro …

d.g: An imperative uttered as a mildly imprecatory or merely expletive introductory exclamation.
d.x: Beshrew your heart, fair daughter!

beshrew.e: From Middle English beschrewen (“to curse, pervert”). By surface analysis, be- + shrew.

d.g: To beset or surround with armed forces for the purpose of compelling to surrender, to lay siege to, beleaguer.
To beleaguer, to vex, to lay siege to, to beset.
To assail or ply, as with requests or demands.

besiege.e: From Middle English besegen, bisegen, equivalent to be- (“around, about”) + siege.

d.g: To smear over, to smear all over, to daub.
To damage the reputation of, to tarnish, to sully.
d.x: His public record is already besmeared with tawdry divorces, […]

besmear.e: From Middle English *bismerwen, from Old English besmirwan, besmierwan (“to besmear”), equivalent to be- + smear. Cognate with Dutch besmeren (“to besmear”), German beschmieren (“to besmear”).

d.g: To make dirty.
To tarnish something, especially someone's reputation.
d.x: The newspaper was on a campaign to besmirch the actor.

besmirch.e: From Middle English besmorchen (attested in besmorchid). Compare Middle English bismotered (“bespattered, soiled”). By surface analysis, be- + smirch.

d.g: To muddle, stupefy, or cause to act foolishly, as with alcoholic liquor or infatuation.
d.x: You expect me and my men to besot ourselves with your drugs, ...

besot.e: From be- + sot. Compare to Middle English assoten, assotten (“to act foolishly; fall madly in love, become infatuated”).

d.g: To cover something with spangles.
d.x: He it was who had bespangled the soils with russet leaves and reeds and who had breathed the breath of life into beings.

bespangle.e: Proto-Indo-European *h₁ep-der. Proto-Indo-European *h₁épsder. Proto-Indo-European *h₁epider. Proto-Indo-European *h₁pi Proto-Germanic *bider. Proto-Germanic *bi- Proto-West Germanic *bi- Old English be- Middle English bi- English be- English spangle English bespangle From be- + spangle.

d.g: To spatter or cover with something; sprinkle with anything liquid, or with any wet or adhesive substance.
To soil by spattering.
d.x: The flour bespattering Squeaker's now neglected clothes spoke eloquently of his clumsy efforts at damper making.

d.g: To asperse with calumny or reproach; shend.

bespatter.e: Proto-Indo-European *h₁ep-der. Proto-Indo-European *h₁épsder. Proto-Indo-European *h₁epider. Proto-Indo-European *h₁pi Proto-Germanic *bider. Proto-Germanic *bi- Proto-West Germanic *bi- Old English be- Middle English bi- English be- English spatter English bespatter From be- + spatter.

d.g: To speak for beforehand; engage in advance; make arrangements for; order or reserve in advance.
d.x: concluding, naturally, that to gratify his avarice was to bespeak his favour

d.g: To stipulate, solicit, ask for, or request, as in a favour.
d.x: to bespeak a calm hearing

d.g: To betoken; show; indicate; depict; foretell; suggest; allude to.
d.x: This act bespeaks his kindness.

d.g: To speak up or out; exclaim; speak.
To speak about; tell of; relate; discuss.
d.x: [They] bespoke dangers […] in order to scare the allies.

d.g: To speak to; address.
d.x: Then ſtaring on her with a ghaſtly Look, / And hollow Voice, he thus the Queen beſpoke.

bespeak.e: From Middle English bespeken, bispeken, from Old English *bespecan, besprecan (“to speak about, speak against, accuse of, claim at law, complain”), from Proto-West Germanic *bisprekan (“to discuss, blame”), from Proto-Germanic *bisprekaną (“to speak about, discuss, blame”), equivalent to be- + speak. …

d.g: To add speckles.
d.x: Seen from the air at night, tiny villages bespeckle the Indian landscape with firefly glows.

bespeckle.e: Proto-Indo-European *h₁ep-der. Proto-Indo-European *h₁épsder. Proto-Indo-European *h₁epider. Proto-Indo-European *h₁pi Proto-Germanic *bider. Proto-Germanic *bi- Proto-West Germanic *bi- Old English be- Middle English bi- English be- English speckle English bespeckle From be- + speckle.

d.g: To make spots on; mark with spots; cover with or as with blots or blemishes.

bespot.e: From Middle English bespotten, equivalent to be- + spot.

d.g: scatter with liquid;  wet lightly

besprinkle.e: From Middle English bisprenklen, bisprenglen, bispringlen, equivalent to be- + sprinkle.

d.g: Alternative form of bestialize.
To make like a beast.
To bring or reduce to the state or condition of a beast.
To put into brisk or vigorous action; to move with life and vigor.
To make active; to rouse oneself.
d.x: The old man and his wife bestirred themselves to make every thing ready for the unexpected guests, […]

d.g: To apply or make use of (someone or something); to employ, to use.
d.x: All the voide time, that is betwene the huores of woorke ſlepe and meat, that they be ſuffered to beſtowe, euerye man as he lyketh beſte hym ſelfe.

d.g: To impart (something) gratuitously; to present (something) to someone or something, especially as a gift or an honour; to confer, to give, to accord; to render.
d.x: I bestow upon you the name of Peter.

d.g: An act of presenting a thing to someone or something, especially as a gift or an honour; a bestowal.
d.x: The Muſes bacely begge, or bibbe, or both, and muſt, for vvhy? / They finde as bad Beſtoe as is their Portage beggerly: / Yea novv by melancholie vvalkes and thred-bare coates vve geſſe / At Clyents and at Poetes: none vvorke more and profit leſſe, […]

bestow.e: PIE word *h₁epi The verb is derived from Middle English bestowen, bistouen, bistowen (“to give, bestow; to apply (something to something else); to arrange or have control over (something); to place (someone) in a position; to use (for some purpose); (reflexive) to find (oneself) a place to live or shelter”) [and other …

b.g: to put (something) away in a suitable place; etc.

d.g: To strew or scatter about; throw or drop here and there.
To strew anything upon; strew over or about; cover or partially cover with things strewn; cover with straw or strewing.

bestrew.e: From Middle English bistrewen, from Old English bestrēawian, bestrēowian (“to bestrew, besprinkle”), equivalent to be- + strew. Cognate with Dutch bestrooien (“to sprinkle, bestrew”), German bestreuen (“to sprinkle, cover”), Swedish beströ (“to strew, sprinkle, scatter”).

d.g: To be astride something, to stand over or sit on with legs on either side, especially to sit on a horse.
d.x:
& thou were the truest frende to thy louar that euer bestrade hors
"And thou were the truest friend to thy lover that ever bestrad horse"

d.g: To stride over, or across.
To dominate.
d.x: Why, man, he doth bestride the narrow world / Like a Colossus[…].

bestride.e: From Middle English bestriden, from Old English bestrīdan, from Proto-West Germanic *bistrīdan; equivalent to be- + stride. Compare Dutch bestrijden, German bestreiten.

d.g: To think of (something or somebody) or that (followed by clause); to remind oneself, to consider, to reflect upon.
d.x: Baſ[ſanio]. Be aſſured you may. / Iew [i.e., Shylock]. I will be aſſured I may: and that I may be aſſured, I will bethinke mee, may I ſpeake with Anthonio?

d.g: To meditate, ponder; to consider.
To determine, resolve.

bethink.e: From Middle English bethenken, bithenchen (“to think about, consider”) from Old English beþenċan, biþenċan (“to think upon, remind, consider, remember”), from Proto-Germanic *biþankijaną; equivalent to be- + think. …

d.g: Often used in a prediction (chiefly in woe betide) or a wish: to happen to (someone or something); to befall.
d.x:
Why, how now, countrymen!
Why flock you thus to me in multitudes?
What accident's betided to the Jews?

d.g: Chiefly in the third person: to happen; to take place; to bechance, to befall.

d.g: A law concerning the frequency distribution of digits in much real-world data, where the number 1 occurs as the leading digit about 30% of the time, and the expected distribution for digits beyond the first approaches a uniform distribution.
d.x: The following argument can give an intuitive feeling for Benford's law.¹¹ Consider a set of numbers x, which are randomly chosen in the interval between 1 and 10. All x between 1 and 1.999 have 1 as the first digit, all x between 2 and 2.999 have 2 as the first digit, and so on. The ratio of the largest and the smallest x is (almost) 2 in the first interval. In the next interval it is 3/2, followed by 4/3, and so on, up to 10/9. The widths of the intervals decrease as in a logarithmic scale. There is more “room” for a number between 1 and 2 than there is between 8 and 9. [In other words, the numbers between 1 and 2 are more dissimilar to one another, quantitatively (regarding how big a factor it takes to get from one to another), than the numbers between other consecutive-integer pairs.]

In particular we will exclude the notion of “observable” in favour of that of “beable”. The beables of the theory are those elements which might correspond to elements of reality, to things which exist. Their existence does not depend on “observation”.
